title: AI to Cut Headcount at More Than Half of UK Firms, CFOs Say
source_used: Bloomberg (first paragraphs only, the rest behind its paywall); BigGo Finance relay of the Bloomberg report; Reuters via Global Banking & Finance Review for the survey sample
key_facts: Deloitte's survey of chief financial officers (CFOs) at large UK companies found 52% expect to cut headcount because of AI (Bloomberg).
AI adoption is still at an early stage: 67% of the CFOs said they have achieved just a quarter of the changes they ultimately expect from AI (Bloomberg).
Bloomberg says many of Britain's large businesses are ready to replace staff with AI over the next year.
Reuters, reporting the same quarterly Deloitte CFO survey, says it polled 66 CFOs, including 12 from FTSE 100 and 25 from FTSE 250 companies, between 17 September and 1 October.
BigGo's relay of the Bloomberg report adds that only about one third of CFOs expect AI to improve profit margins within the next year (not seen in the Bloomberg text we could open).
Deloitte published the survey on Wednesday 14 Oct 2026; Bloomberg's report went out on the evening of 13 Oct.
quote_evidence: Deloitte said Wednesday that 52% of CFOs expect to cut headcount due to the technology, with AI adoption still in its early stages.
More than two thirds — 67% — said they've achieved just a quarter of the changes they ultimately expect from AI.
Many of Britain's large businesses are ready to replace staff with artificial intelligence over the next year, according to a prominent survey of chief financial officers.
why_it_matters_hint: More than half of surveyed finance chiefs at large UK firms expect AI to reduce their headcount within a year, though adoption is early.
event_date: Deloitte survey run 17 Sep to 1 Oct 2026; published 14 Oct 2026 (Bloomberg report 13 Oct)
notes: Bloomberg's page gave only its first two paragraphs (417 characters, paywall). Deloitte's own press page returned 404. The headline and summary use only facts in the Bloomberg text; the sample size and dates come from Reuters's report of the same survey. Survey measures expectations, not cuts made.
